clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme beta-galactosidase, leading to accumulation of GM1 ganglioside and related substrates in neurons and other tissues
The infantile form combines features of a gangliosidosis and a storage disorder, with neurodegeneration together with coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal changes
A cherry-red macular spot may be present in a substantial proportion of infantile cases
Dysostosis multiplex on skeletal imaging overlaps with the mucopolysaccharidoses, reflecting glycosaminoglycan storage
Late-infantile/juvenile and adult forms exist, with the adult form often presenting with dystonia and slower progression and fewer somatic features
The same enzyme deficiency underlies Morquio syndrome type B, which is predominantly a skeletal phenotype with preserved intellect
Hypotonia and developmental regression dominate the early infantile presentation, later progressing to spasticity and seizures
No curative therapy is established, so management is supportive with genetic counselling for families
reference.pathophysiology: GM1 gangliosidosis results from biallelic pathogenic variants in GLB1, encoding lysosomal beta-galactosidase. Deficient enzyme activity impairs removal of terminal galactose residues, causing accumulation of GM1 ganglioside within neurons and of galactose-containing oligosaccharides and keratan sulfate in visceral and skeletal tissues. Neuronal ganglioside storage drives progressive neurodegeneration, while systemic substrate accumulation produces the organomegaly and dysostosis that overlap with the mucopolysaccharidoses. The severity and phenotype depend on residual enzyme activity, spanning severe infantile disease to milder adult-onset forms.
additionalDifferentials: Mucopolysaccharidoses given the shared dysostosis and coarse features
Niemann-Pick disease and other storage disorders with organomegaly
Other causes of infantile neurodegeneration with cherry-red spot
Morquio syndrome type B for the skeletal-predominant phenotype
additionalInvestigations: Assay of beta-galactosidase enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
GLB1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Rapid neurodevelopmental regression in an infant with organomegaly
Emerging seizures or feeding and swallowing difficulty
Progressive dystonia in juvenile or adult presentations
Cardiac involvement in more severe phenotypes
reference.prognosis: The infantile form is severe and progressive, typically fatal in early childhood. Late-infantile and juvenile forms progress more slowly, and the adult form has a protracted course often dominated by movement disorder. No disease-modifying therapy is currently established, so care is supportive.
pitfalls: Confusing it with a mucopolysaccharidosis because of the shared skeletal and facial features
Not distinguishing it from the GM2 gangliosidoses without enzyme testing
Overlooking the milder adult dystonic form
Failing to provide genetic counselling to at-risk relatives
management: Provide supportive symptomatic care as no disease-modifying enzyme or gene therapy is currently established
Control seizures with antiseizure medication tailored to seizure type
Optimise nutrition and airway safety with feeding support and gastrostomy where dysphagia and aspiration risk develop
Manage spasticity and dystonia with muscle relaxants, physiotherapy and, in the adult movement-predominant form, targeted movement-disorder therapy
Provide respiratory care with chest physiotherapy and prompt treatment of aspiration and recurrent infection
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology, metabolic, ophthalmology and palliative care, and offer genetic counselling with carrier and prenatal testing for autosomal recessive GLB1 disease
